He had been CEO of the company ever since he founded it on April 5, 1993. Nvidia started out as a graphics card company; Huang’s exit — nominally because of affairs with a buyer who may or may not have been a Chinese spy, as well as at least two company employees — was ultimately because Nvidia was, by the powers that be, considered a defense contractor, and Huang never adjusted. In this, Huang was the ultimate victim of his own success. Nvidia’s first graphics cards simply translated triangles into pixels. The 2001 GeForce 3 introduced a programmable pixel shader, which meant a video card’s functionality was no longer pre-defined. The killer move, however — which almost killed the company — was the 2006 introduction of CUDA, which was an API for programming those shaders. For much of the next 16 years Huang sold the gospel of CUDA , convinced it was the platform for a future of accelerated computing; then, in 2022, came ChatGPT. ChatGPT made clear what GPUs were most useful for: large language models, and Nvidia made the best GPUs. More than that, Huang had realized that the future of accelerated computing was not just chips, but rather systems; that drove the purchase of Mellanox in 2019, which provided the technology for Nvidia to scale out from chips, setting it down the road to being the best option for the sort of large scale training that made large language models possible. For this Nvidia charged very high prices, with margins exceeding 70%, because they could: they had the platform, the technology, and, over the past few years as others sought to make their own chips, the supply chain. Huang’s impact on the Asian supply chain in particular cannot be overstated. Byrne Hobart, in his book Boom: Bubbles and the End of Stagnation , notes that one of the benefits of bubbles is that they provide a coordination function, as the fear of missing out incentivizes multiple entities with interlocking dependencies to all commit to building at the same time; Huang was, in many respects, a one-person coordination function. Huang gave multiple keynotes a year, which he explained as how he communicated with the ecosystem broadly, and was famous for eating and drinking his way across Asia in particular, convincing reluctant suppliers that the AI boom was real, and locking up the lion’s share of their output for Nvidia and its stunning commitment to a yearly release cycle. Huang, who had toiled for decades in relative obscurity, known primarily to gamers, and only barely to the tech industry, became a rock star, swarmed wherever he went, always in his black leather jacket. He also, to his ultimate detriment, became a political figure. Nvidia had long had no presence in either Washington D.C. or Beijing , and was blindsided by the Biden administration’s imposition of chip controls in 2022. Nvidia’s immediate reaction to those initial controls, which restricted exports based on interconnect speed, was to immediately release the A800 in China, which was an A100 with a third of its interconnects disabled. That set the tone for the conflict that I believe was the true cause of Huang’s downfall: Huang strenuously disagreed with the various iterations of the chip ban, and Nvidia only bothered to do the bare minimum to abide by the letter of the law, never the spirit. That approach, in all likelihood, extended to Nvidia’s oversight (or lack thereof) of Singaporean entities that were alleged to be fronts for chips for China. Some of these were legal: Chinese companies are allowed to access cloud computing facilities outside of China that house leading edge Nvidia chips, although chip control advocates are seeking to close that loophole; some were not legal, in that the chips were ultimately ferried to China. Megaspeed, whose executive, Alice Huang, was the first person Huang was alleged to have an affair with, was officially in the former business, and alleged to actually be in the latter. There are whispers that Megaspeed’s ultimate customer was not, or not just, Alibaba, but also the Chinese military. These are whispers, to be clear; it was the affairs that were enough, at least publicly, to lead to Huang’s resignation. Nvidia, Most Valuable Company in the World, 2024–2026 Nvidia’s durability — at least that of their margins — was already an open question. Start with CUDA: when the market was software written for GPUs, a platform — including not just an API but a huge set of libraries targeting every conceivable market for accelerated computing — was a nearly impenetrable moat. That is why LLMs like GPT were written using CUDA. LLMs, though, both brought Nvidia its incredible success, and also seeded its greatest risks. The first is that the vast majority of developer energy moved up the stack, using the LLM’s API as a platform; for most companies, CUDA didn’t matter.
